title: It is the Human Intuition, Stupid: Exploring Human Factors on Reliance in Human-AI Decision-Making
authors: Chen, V.; Lee, S.; Wong, S.; Kim, P.
venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT)
tldr: A user study of 490 participants across three domains found that intuitive thinking and overconfidence in personal judgment significantly predicted unjustified reliance on human experts over AI advisors, highlighting that understanding human cognition is critical for effective human-AI collaboration.
problem_and_motivation: Research on human-AI collaboration often focuses on system-side factors like explainability and fairness while overlooking human-side factors such as intuition and cognitive biases. There is limited understanding of how individual differences in intuitive versus analytical thinking styles influence reliance on AI systems. This gap can lead to suboptimal decision-making outcomes when humans either over-rely on or under-rely on AI recommendations.
approach: Controlled user study with 490 participants across three domains: loan approval, academic paper acceptance, and recidivism prediction.
Participants completed pre-experiments measuring cognitive style (Intuitive Thinking Scale) and domain knowledge, then made decisions with and without AI advice.
Three factors were manipulated: advice type (human expert vs. AI advisor), AI reliability (90 percent vs. 75 percent), and problem type (subjective vs. objective).
Dependent variables measured were acceptance rate, accuracy, advice-taking rate, and agreement rate.
Statistical analysis used chi-square tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, binary logistic regression, and multi-group mediation analysis to test hypotheses.
findings: Intuitive thinking and overconfidence significantly and negatively predicted unjustified reliance on human expert advisors.
In the loan approval domain, intuitive thinking significantly predicted unjustified reliance on human experts but not on AI advisors.
AI advisors with 90 percent reliability had a significantly higher acceptance rate (66.4 percent) than human experts (58.8 percent).
Participants with high domain knowledge were significantly more likely to disagree with AI advisors who provided incorrect recommendations.
The negative relationship between intuitive thinking and unjustified reliance was mediated by overconfidence in personal judgment.

definitions.definition: Accepting incorrect advice from an AI or human advisor when it leads to a wrong decision outcome.
Rejecting incorrect advice from an AI or human advisor, maintaining the correct decision.
The tendency to engage analytical thinking and suppress intuitive responses in decision-making.
A cognitive bias where an individuals confidence in their own judgment exceeds their actual accuracy.

topics.name: Trust, Usability, and Transparency in Financial Tools
topics.justification: Directly investigates how trust in human advisors vs. AI advisors influences decision-making in financial contexts like loan approval.

topics.name: Transparency of AI Models
topics.justification: Explores how AI advisor transparency and reliability affect user reliance and decision quality in human-AI collaboration.

topics.name: Predictive Modeling in Personal Finance Systems
topics.justification: The loan approval experiment directly involves financial decision-making with predictive AI models.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper makes a significant contribution to human-AI collaboration research by demonstrating that human-side cognitive factors—specifically intuitive thinking and overconfidence—are stronger predictors of unjustified reliance than system-side factors like AI explainability. The study provides empirical evidence that the same cognitive factors affect reliance differently depending on whether the advisor is human or AI, and that domain knowledge moderates these effects. This highlights the critical importance of understanding human cognition for designing effective AI-assisted decision-making systems.
directly_justifies: Intuitive thinking significantly predicts unjustified reliance on human expert advisors but not necessarily on AI advisors.
Overconfidence in personal judgment mediates the relationship between intuitive thinking and unjustified reliance.
Higher domain knowledge leads to greater rejection of incorrect AI recommendations.
limits: WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) participant sample limits generalizability.
Simulated laboratory setting may not fully capture real-world decision-making complexity.
The study did not measure how AI explanations influence reliance over time.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All topic domains were systematically scanned. Domains 9.A and 9.B are highly relevant as the paper directly investigates trust and transparency in AI-assisted decision-making, particularly in a financial context. Domain 6.A is medium relevance due to the loan approval experiment involving financial predictive modeling. Domains 1-5, 7-8, 10-14 were considered and rejected: the paper does not address Filipino demographics, budgeting, gambling, savings, debt, fraud detection, addiction, synthetic data, or debt reduction. The paper is focused on human cognition and AI collaboration, not personal finance management.

limitations: WEIRD participant sample limits cross-cultural generalizability.
Simulated decision-making tasks may not reflect real-world complexity and stakes.
The study does not address how AI explanations might mitigate intuitive thinking biases over time.
remember_this: Intuitive thinking and overconfidence predict unjustified reliance on human experts over AI advisors.
Domain knowledge helps users reject incorrect AI recommendations.
AI advisors with high reliability achieve higher acceptance rates than human experts.
Understanding human cognition is critical for effective human-AI collaboration.
The same cognitive factors affect reliance differently for human vs. AI advisors.
